deep.reconstruction:
Context. Together with the previous page (a table of p = N(a+bρ) for p = 7, …, 73) and the next page (power tables mod 8−ρ, 7−2ρ, 5−4ρ, and a programme for computing in Z[x]/(1+x+x²)), this page is part of Gauss's work on the arithmetic of the Eisenstein integers Z[ρ] (ρ² + ρ + 1 = 0) and on cubic and quadratic residues there. The norm is N(a+bρ) = a² − ab + b².

(A) Coloured diagram 'Schema für 43'. It shows the hexagonal lattice Z[ρ] with large triangles and hexagonal regions washed in three colours (green, pink/red, yellow). On the previous page 43 = N(6−ρ). The most plausible reading is a tiling of the lattice by complete residue systems mod 6−ρ (each of 43 points), coloured by residue class, probably by cubic character since there are three colours. The strong red region would be a chosen fundamental, least-residue domain. I did not verify this from the image point by point.

(B) The list of primes continues the previous page. Each p ≡ 1 (mod 6) is written as the norm of a+bρ:
- 79 = N(7−3ρ), 97 = N(8−3ρ), 103 = N(9−2ρ), 109 = N(7−5ρ), 127 = N(7−6ρ)
- 139 = N(10−3ρ), 151 = N(9−5ρ), 157 = N(12−ρ)
- 163: left blank on the page; the representation is 11−3ρ
- 181 = N(11−4ρ), 193 = N(9−7ρ); here ρ is omitted in the writing.

(C) Normalisation. 'p(−ρ)^k fiat = p' ≡ 1 mod (2−2ρ)' means: multiply the prime by the unit (−ρ)^k so that it becomes ≡ 1 mod 2(1−ρ). The ideal 2(1−ρ) has norm 12, and (Z[ρ]/2(1−ρ))* has order 6. So the six units represent it exactly and the associate is unique. This is the analogue of Gauss's biquadratic normalisation ≡ 1 mod (2+2i). It differs from Eisenstein's 'primary' (≡ 2 mod 3). A prime is also written in three coordinates, α + βρ + γρρ.

(D) Table headed 1−ρ, giving the quadratic character of 1−ρ modulo the normalised prime π:
- 7: π = −3−2ρ, N
- 13: π = −1−4ρ, N
- 19: π = 3−2ρ, R
- 31: π = 1+6ρ, N. The page or transcription has 1−6ρ, whose norm is 43, so it must be 1+6ρ.

Check, mine. With ρ ≡ r mod π:
- p = 7: r = 2, 1−ρ ≡ −1, a non-residue.
- p = 13: r = 3, 1−ρ ≡ −2, a non-residue.
- p = 19: r = 11, 1−ρ ≡ 9 = 3², a residue.
- p = 31: r = 5, 1−ρ ≡ −4, a non-residue.
All four entries are correct.

(E) Proposed criterion: '1−ρ is a quadratic residue of p if p(1−ρ)(1−ρ) ≡ ±(1.4.7 ; 7.7.10) mod 12, a non-residue if ≡ ±(1.1.10 ; 1.7.4) mod 12.'

My reconstruction. Write π(1−ρ)² = Aρ⁰ + Bρ + Cρ² in the canonical sum-zero form, with
- A = α+β−2γ
- B = −2α+β+γ
- C = α−2β+γ.
All of Gauss's triples have entries ≡ 1 mod 3 and sum ≡ 0 mod 12, consistent with this. For normalised π, every entry is ≡ 1 mod 3, and the triple mod 12 depends only on π mod 4. Since (1−ρ)² = −3ρ, the criterion is really a condition on π mod 4.

The correct law, mine (checked numerically for p = 7, 13, 19, 31, 37, 43, 61, 67, 73):
- 1−ρ is a quadratic residue of π iff π ≡ 1 or 3+2ρ (mod 4);
- it is a non-residue iff π ≡ 3 or 1+2ρ (mod 4).

Canonical triples of π(1−ρ)² mod 12 for the four classes:
- π ≡ 1: (1,10,1), R
- π ≡ 3: (7,10,7), N
- π ≡ 1+2ρ: (7,4,1), N
- π ≡ 3+2ρ: (1,4,7), R

Gauss's (1,4,7) for R matches exactly, as for p = 19. His (1,7,4) for N is a cyclic shift of (7,4,1), as for p = 7 and 31. His (7,7,10) and (1,1,10) are cyclic shifts of the π ≡ 3 and π ≡ 1 classes, but he labels them R and N respectively, the reverse of the truth. Underlying fact, mine: 1−ρ = ρ²(ρ−ρ²) = ρ²√−3, so the criterion is a supplementary law for the quadratic character of √−3 in Z[ρ]. For p ≡ 1 (mod 12) this is equivalent to the biquadratic character of −3.

(F) Boxed note: 'Giebt den Zahlen die Form x + y√A' ('gives the numbers the form x+y√A'). This signals the intended generalisation to quadratic irrationalities.
errors: The prime for 31 is written (or transcribed) as 1−6ρ, but N(1−6ρ) = 43. The correct normalised prime is 1+6ρ: N = 31, ≡ 1 mod 2 and 7 ≡ 1 mod 3.
163 is listed without a representation; 163 = N(11−3ρ).

In the mod-12 criterion, under the natural reading (canonical triple of π(1−ρ)², cyclic shifts allowed), the triples (7.7.10) and (1.1.10) are assigned the wrong characters. (7.7.10) corresponds to π ≡ 3 mod 4, a non-residue: compare Gauss's own example 13, π = −1−4ρ, triple (7,10,7), N. (1.1.10) corresponds to π ≡ 1 mod 4, a residue: example 37, π = −7−4ρ. The entries (1.4.7) R and (1.7.4) N are right. This may also be a matter of a coordinate convention I cannot recover, so it is flagged as uncertain.
The '±' in the criterion is redundant or misleading for normalised π. All entries are ≡ 1 mod 3, and negatives would be ≡ 2 mod 3.

results.what: Representation of primes p ≡ 1 mod 6 (79 to 193) as norms a² − ab + b² of Eisenstein integers.
results.modern_name: Splitting of primes in Z[ρ] / representation by x² − xy + y²

results.what: Normalisation of an Eisenstein prime by a unit so that π ≡ 1 mod 2(1−ρ), unique because the units represent (Z[ρ]/(2−2ρ))*.
results.modern_name: Choice of primary associates (Gauss-type normalisation, analogue of ≡ 1 mod (2+2i))
results.usually_credited_to: Eisenstein (1844) for cubic primary elements; Gauss for the Gaussian analogue

results.what: Table and mod-12 (effectively mod 4) criterion for the quadratic character of 1−ρ (equivalently √−3) modulo an Eisenstein prime π.
results.modern_name: Supplementary law of quadratic reciprocity in Z[ρ]; equivalent for p ≡ 1 mod 12 to the quartic character of −3
results.usually_credited_to: Quadratic reciprocity in number fields: Hilbert/Hecke. Quartic character of −3 (and 3): Lehmer, Emma; Lemmermeyer surveys.

results.what: Coloured geometric 'Schema' of the Eisenstein lattice modulo the prime 6−ρ of norm 43, probably showing residue systems and cubic classes.
results.modern_name: Fundamental domain / tiling of a lattice by residue classes; visualisation of cubic residue character
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (geometric representation of complex residues in his biquadratic work)

deep.surprise_reason: Gauss's private work on cubic residues and arithmetic in Z[ρ] is known from the Nachlass, and the normalisation and prime list are routine. The less familiar items are an explicit, partly correct supplementary criterion for the quadratic character of 1−ρ (√−3) in Z[ρ], and a carefully coloured lattice diagram mod 43. Both are notable details rather than major new results.

checkable.asserts: Each listed a+bρ has norm p, including the missing 163 = N(11−3ρ).
The normalised primes for 7, 13, 19 have the right norms; 1+6ρ has norm 31, while 1−6ρ has norm 43, so the 31 entry must be 1+6ρ.
Each π = a+bρ in the table is ≡ 1 mod 2 and ≡ 1 mod (1−ρ), i.e. ≡ 1 mod 2(1−ρ).
Euler's criterion for 1−ρ, with ρ ≡ r mod π, gives N, N, R, N for 7, 13, 19, 31, matching Gauss's table.
The residues r used for ρ mod π are roots of x²+x+1 mod p.
Further data for the criterion: π = −7−4ρ (37) R, 7+6ρ (43) R, 5−4ρ (61) R, −7+2ρ (67) N, −9−8ρ (73) N. This supports: R iff π ≡ 1 or 3+2ρ mod 4.
Canonical sum-zero coefficient triples of π(1−ρ)² mod 12 for π = a+bρ (γ = 0), used to compare with Gauss's list (1.4.7), (7.7.10), (1.1.10), (1.7.4).

transcription_corrections: '31 | 1−6ρ' should read 1+6ρ; the norm of 1−6ρ is 43.
'181 11−4' and '193 9−7' mean 11−4ρ and 9−7ρ; ρ is omitted on the page.
'N.R' in the last line is 'Non-Residuum'; 'R quadr.' means 'quadratic residue'.
The heading numbers '216', 'Ma[?] noth.[?]' and the pencilled 'U' are archival or old foliation marks, not mathematics.
